name: Der von Kürenberg
credit: Der von Kürenberg, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Der von Kürenberg, the earliest named lyric poet of the German minnesong, was active in the Danube region around the middle of the twelfth century and is known for his short long-line stanzas, among them the celebrated falcon song.
Seven of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poems.title: Nunc Amet
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
To use dear friends as strangers, a sorry thing it is!
Who to his friend holds closely, praise is surely his;
I am fain of that custom.
Bid him to love me dearly, as in times gone past,
And mind him of the words we spoke when I looked upon him last.

poems.title: The Message
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
"Dear love, of what sore sorrow wilt thou now warn me?
The day of our parting may I ne'er live to see!
If thou shalt cease to love me,
I shall let all folk near me see full clearly then
That no joy whatsoever I find in all other men."

poems.title: Night Thoughts
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
"When in my night-dress I stand all alone,
And when I think upon thee, noble knight, thereon
Bright grows my face, as blossoms the rose upon the thorn,
And the heart within me is sad and fain to mourn."

poems.title: The Falcon
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
Full often hath it grieved me and brought my heart sore pain,
That what I ever longed for I never yet could gain
Nor e'er may hope to win it; a hapless case is this;
Yet I mean not gold nor silver; of mortal shape and look it is.

To rear me up a falcon more than a year I spent.
When I at length had tamed him all to my content
And fairly in his feathers had twisted golden strands,
Up in the air he mounted and flew away to other lands.

Since then I saw my falcon, and fairly did he soar;
Thongs of silken riband on his feet he bore,
And bright were all his feathers, golden-red to see.
May God send those together, whoso fond lovers fain would be!

poems.title: Departure
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
Now bring me quick my charger and coat of mail to hand,
Since all for a lady I must leave the land.
She would fain constrain me my love to her to give;
Love of mine she never shall get, as long as she doth live.

poems.title: Secret Love
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
Lo, the star of evening hides its brightness now!
Fair lady, if thou see me, even so do thou!
Then upon some other man let thy glances go,
And how it stands between us there's never any man shall know!

poems.title: The Snare of the Fowler
poems.author: Der von Kürenberg
poems.text:
Women, even as falcons, full quickly tamed are they!
If ye but lure them rightly, they come to hand straightway.
So was a lovely lady wooed by a gallant knight;
Whene'er I think upon it, my heart is high for delight.
